beats.text: It's eighteen hundred. Mary wants her room as bright as yours, for just one hour.
That one hour of light will cost her almost six hours of work.
Light came from candles made of animal fat.
But for five hundred years, its price barely moved.
So for most people, the day ended at sunset.
Then came gas lamps, kerosene, and the light bulb.
Today, the same light costs you less than half a second of work.
Mary's six hours of work are your half a second.

sources: Labour time for 1,000 lumen-hours (about one bright modern bulb for one hour): tallow candles around 1800 about 5.4 hours of work; 1992 about 0.00012 hours (= 0.43 seconds). William D. Nordhaus (1996), 'Do Real-Output and Real-Wage Measures Capture Reality? The History of Lighting Suggests Not', in Bresnahan & Gordon (eds.), The Economics of New Goods, NBER/University of Chicago Press; figures as summarised by HumanProgress.org ('Lighting costs near nothing now'). One candle gives about 1 candela = about 12.6 lumens -> 1,000 lumen-hours = about 75–80 candle-hours.

Price line on the wall: price of lighting in the UK, constant 2000 British pounds per million lumen-hours, 1301–2006, Fouquet & Pearson (2006), The Energy Journal, via Our World in Data (1301: 33,043; 1800: 9,540; 2006: 2.89; log scale).

Mary is illustrative (a typical worker, not a real person). 'The day ended at sunset' for most people: general historical description; evening light was a luxury (Nordhaus 1996; Fouquet & Pearson 2006).
